summary: Sirach 49 continues the praise of Israel's ancestors by honoring Josiah, then explaining Judah's collapse after kings abandoned the law of the Most High. It remembers Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the twelve prophets, Zerubbabel, Jesus son of Josedek, Nehemiah, and finally figures from earlier memory: Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth, and Adam.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Sirach's praise of ancestors reads Israel's past as moral memory: leaders are evaluated by faithfulness, reform, rebuilding, and hope. It also moves from the fall of Judah to restoration figures, keeping ruin and renewal in the same historical sequence.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews who wanted instruction shaped by Israel's law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with the temple, priesthood, ancestral writings, and scribal instruction central to the book's world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction and poetic praise of ancestors, here using compact historical encomium.

outline.heading: Josiah Remembered
outline.note: Josiah's memory is compared to incense, honey, and music because he reformed the people and set his heart toward the Lord.

outline.heading: Judah's Kings and Jerusalem's Ruin
outline.note: Apart from David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, the kings are judged as wicked; their failure leads to lost power, foreign rule, and the burning of the chosen city.

outline.heading: Prophets in Judgment and Hope
outline.note: Jeremiah is described as mistreated yet appointed as prophet; Ezekiel sees divine glory; the twelve prophets are remembered with hope for Jacob.

outline.heading: Builders After Disaster
outline.note: Zerubbabel, Jesus son of Josedek, and Nehemiah are praised for rebuilding the house, raising fallen walls, and restoring houses.

outline.heading: Ancient Honored Figures
outline.note: The chapter closes by naming Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth, and Adam as uniquely honored figures in human memory.

keyVerses.text: He set his heart right toward the Lord. In lawless days, he made godliness prevail.
keyVerses.why: This sums up the chapter's praise of Josiah: his reform is described as inner direction toward the Lord and public resistance to lawlessness.

keyVerses.text: They set the chosen city of the sanctuary on fire and made her streets desolate, as it was written by the hand of Jeremiah.
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the chapter's turn from praise of Josiah to the disaster that followed Judah's unfaithful kings.

keyVerses.text: Also of the twelve prophets, may their bones flourish again out of their place. He comforted the people of Jacob, and delivered them by confident hope.
keyVerses.why: The verse gathers the prophetic memory around comfort and hope, not only warning and destruction.

keyVerses.text: Also of Nehemiah the memory is great. He raised up for us fallen walls, set up the gates and bars, and rebuilt our houses.
keyVerses.why: Nehemiah represents the chapter's restoration movement: after city and streets are desolate, walls, gates, bars, and houses are rebuilt.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with Josiah?
questions.answer: Sirach praises Josiah as a model king whose memory is pleasant and enduring. The chapter says he reformed the people, removed abominations, set his heart toward the Lord, and made godliness prevail in lawless days.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by “the memory of Josiah”?
questions.answer: “Memory” here means the remembered reputation of Josiah among later readers and worshipers. Sirach compares that memory to incense, honey, and music, so the point is not merely that Josiah is known, but that his remembered life is treasured.

questions.question: Why are David, Hezekiah, and Josiah singled out?
questions.answer: The chapter names these three as exceptions among the kings it judges. It says the others were wicked because they abandoned the law of the Most High, and then says the kings of Judah came to an end.

questions.question: Does Sirach say exactly how Judah fell?
questions.answer: The chapter gives a theological and moral summary rather than a full historical account. It says the kings abandoned the law, gave their power and glory to others, and that the chosen city was burned and made desolate.

questions.question: Why mention Jeremiah after the burned city?
questions.answer: Verse 6 connects the city's burning and desolate streets with what was written “by the hand of Jeremiah.” Verse 7 then remembers Jeremiah as mistreated, yet set apart from the womb to be a prophet whose work included both tearing down and building up.

questions.question: What is difficult about the line on Jeremiah being “sanctified in the womb”?
questions.answer: The phrase describes Jeremiah as set apart for a prophetic calling before birth. It recalls Jeremiah 1:5 and is followed here by the work of rooting out, destroying, building, and planting. Sirach uses the line to underline the authority of the prophet whom Jerusalem mistreated; it does not develop a general account of how divine choice and human action relate.

questions.question: What does Ezekiel see in this chapter?
questions.answer: Sirach says Ezekiel saw “the vision of glory,” which God showed him on “the chariot of the cherubim.” The chapter does not retell the vision; it identifies Ezekiel by this striking experience of divine glory.

questions.question: Who are the builders praised after the prophets?
questions.answer: Zerubbabel is compared to a signet ring on the right hand. Jesus son of Josedek is remembered with him for building the house and exalting a people holy to the Lord, and Nehemiah is praised for raising fallen walls, setting gates and bars, and rebuilding houses.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end with Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth, and Adam?
questions.answer: After praising kings, prophets, and rebuilders, the chapter reaches back to earlier figures of ancestral memory. Each is honored briefly: Enoch was taken from the earth, Joseph supported his people, Shem and Seth were honored, and Adam is placed above every living thing in the creation.

glossary.def: A king remembered in this chapter for reforming the people, removing abominations, and setting his heart toward the Lord.
A title for God in verse 4, where abandoning the law of the Most High explains the judgment on Judah's kings.
The city of the sanctuary in verse 6, remembered as burned and made desolate.
Heavenly beings associated here with the chariot on which Ezekiel saw the vision of glory.
A valued seal-ring used as an image of honor for Zerubbabel in verse 11.
